paragraphs: FlowDPO tackles the generation of accurate three-dimensional atomic structures. Generative models offer a way to predict these structures, but the paper identifies two problems: limited exploration of the probability paths used for generation and persistent hallucinations during sampling. Its approach combines flow matching with preference-based refinement to improve the generated structures.

The process starts with a pretrained flow matching model that produces several candidate structures for each training example. Those candidates are ranked by their distance from the known reference structure. This creates an automatic preference dataset, which Direct Preference Optimization then uses to refine the original model toward structures closer to the desired reference distribution.

The theoretical analysis establishes that the framework and its objective work with arbitrary Gaussian probability paths. That compatibility gives the method flexibility within this family of paths. Experiments on antibodies and crystals report substantial benefits, supporting the use of automatically constructed structural preferences to improve generation in both studied settings.
neurips-2024-3d-structure-prediction-of-.tldr: FlowDPO improves atomic structure generation by refining flow matching models with automatically ranked candidate structures.

paragraphs: Clustering often needs to satisfy more than one definition of a good grouping. For example, areas on a map may need to be geographically compact while also grouping districts with similar data. These goals can conflict, so choosing a clustering requires understanding the available compromises between them.

This paper develops algorithms that approximately compute Pareto-optimal sets for several pairs of clustering objectives. Such a set describes trade-offs where improving one objective comes at a cost to the other. The combinations studied include optimizing k-center and k-means together, as well as using k-center with two different distance measures.

The algorithms come with provable approximation guarantees, giving a mathematical basis for the quality of the trade-offs they recover. Experiments also show that these approximate Pareto sets contain useful clusterings that optimizing either objective alone does not find. The contribution is therefore a way to expose meaningful choices between competing goals, rather than requiring a single objective to determine the entire solution.
neurips-2024-approximately-pareto-optima.tldr: Provably approximate Pareto sets reveal useful clustering trade-offs that optimizing one objective alone can miss.

paragraphs: A language model can express different, even contradictory, stereotypes about the same profession across contexts. This paper argues that measuring only a model's average tendency misses part of its discrimination risk. It introduces the Bias-Volatility Framework to represent stereotypes through a probability distribution that captures both their direction and their variability.

The framework measures the likelihood and extent of outputs that disadvantage vulnerable groups. It then mathematically separates aggregated discrimination risk into bias risk, associated with the distribution's mean, and volatility risk, associated with its variation. This makes inconsistent generation an explicit part of the assessment rather than something averaged away.

Across 12 evaluated models, bias risk was the main contributor to discrimination risk, and most models showed substantial pro-male stereotypes across nearly all careers. Reinforcement learning from human feedback reduced discrimination through lower bias while increasing volatility. The study also found correlations with socioeconomic factors such as salaries. These findings describe the evaluated models and show why improvements in average bias need to be interpreted alongside changes in variability.
neurips-2024-bias-and-volatility-a-stati.tldr: The Bias-Volatility Framework separates stereotype-related discrimination risk into average bias and variation across generated outputs.

paragraphs: Con4m addresses classification of consecutive segments within time series that contain several classes lasting for different durations. In this setting, neighboring segments have temporal dependencies that can help identify their classes. Treating every segment as an independent example overlooks that context and leaves useful information outside the classification process.

The paper also addresses disagreement about where one class ends and another begins. Annotators with different expertise can assign inconsistent boundary labels, which can destabilize models designed around clean labels. The authors first formally establish that valuable context can improve the ability to distinguish classes, then build a consistency-learning framework around that insight.

Con4m uses contextual prior information at both the data and label levels. It draws on relationships among consecutive segments while harmonizing inconsistent boundary labels during training. Experiments across multiple datasets support its effectiveness for this segmented classification setting. The findings connect two aspects of the same temporal structure: context can help interpret a segment, and it can also help handle ambiguity in the labels near class transitions.
neurips-2024-con4m-context-aware-consist.tldr: Con4m uses temporal context and label consistency to improve classification of neighboring time-series segments with uncertain boundaries.

paragraphs: Subgraph-based drug interaction models must decide which parts of a graph to examine and how to represent those parts for prediction. These choices influence the information available to the model. Although such methods have shown effectiveness and interpretability, manually customizing their selection and encoding components can be expensive.

This paper adapts the idea of neural architecture search to discover components suited to the available drug interaction data. It defines broad search spaces for both subgraph selection and encoding, allowing the search to consider different interaction contexts. The goal is to find useful combinations of what the model examines and how it processes that information.

Exploring all those possibilities brings a large search space and costly sampling. The proposed relaxation mechanism uses an approximation strategy to make exploration more efficient. Extensive experiments report effectiveness and superiority for the method, while the discovered subgraphs and encoding functions illustrate its adaptability. The result supports automated customization as a practical approach to components that would otherwise require substantial manual adjustment.
neurips-2024-customized-subgraph-selecti.tldr: An automated search customizes subgraph selection and encoding for drug interaction prediction while reducing the cost of exploring candidate designs.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can represent complex distributions that are useful in reinforcement learning, but generating samples often takes many iterative steps. That inference cost creates an obstacle when using them to support decisions. Diffusion Spectral Representation, or Diff-SR, investigates how to obtain their representational benefits without relying on expensive diffusion sampling.

The framework uses a connection between diffusion models and energy-based models to extract representations for value functions. These representations are described as sufficient for value functions in both fully observable Markov decision processes and partially observable ones. The focus is therefore on retaining information needed to evaluate decisions, rather than directly generating samples through the diffusion process.

The paper shows how these representations support efficient policy optimization and practical algorithms that bypass diffusion sampling and its inference cost. Empirical studies cover benchmarks with both full and partial observability and report robust, advantageous performance. Together, the theoretical framework and experiments support representation learning as another route for applying expressive diffusion models to reinforcement learning.
neurips-2024-diffusion-spectral-represen.tldr: Diff-SR extracts value-function representations from diffusion models to support reinforcement learning without costly diffusion sampling.

paragraphs: Elliptical Attention changes how a transformer decides which input tokens deserve attention. The paper links conventional dot-product attention to a Euclidean view of similarity and identifies problems with representation collapse and sensitivity to contaminated samples. Its proposed remedy is to make the geometry of attention reflect directions that matter in the current context.

The method computes attention weights using a Mahalanobis distance. This stretches the feature space along contextually relevant directions and creates an ellipsoidal neighborhood around each query. Tokens positioned along those important directions receive greater weight, allowing the attention mechanism to emphasize relevant information through its choice of distance measure.

The authors present two benefits: less representation collapse and greater robustness. Their explanation is that attention can use contextually relevant information more broadly instead of concentrating on a small subset of informative features. Experiments compare the method with dot-product attention and other leading attention approaches on object classification, image segmentation, and language modeling. The reported advantages across these tasks support the usefulness of adapting attention geometry across visual and language data.
neurips-2024-elliptical-attention-afa8d3.tldr: Elliptical Attention uses context-sensitive distance geometry to reduce representation collapse and improve robustness in evaluated vision and language tasks.

paragraphs: This paper separates two reasons a prediction can be uncertain: insufficient training knowledge and uncertainty inherent in the task. The first, epistemic uncertainty, can decrease with more training data. The second, aleatoric uncertainty, concerns variability inherent to the problem. Distinguishing them is especially valuable in applications such as medical imaging and weather forecasting.

An ensemble of conditional diffusion models offers a conceptually straightforward way to estimate both kinds of uncertainty, but training many large models can become computationally intractable. Hyper-diffusion models, called HyperDM, introduce an approach to ensembling that estimates both uncertainty components using a single model.

The reported prediction accuracy matches multi-model ensembles and sometimes exceeds them, while uncertainty estimates improve over existing methods. The approach also scales to modern architectures such as Attention U-Net. Validation covers x-ray computed tomography reconstruction and temperature forecasting. These results support the possibility of obtaining both strong predictions and useful uncertainty separation without training a separate collection of full models in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-estimating-epistemic-and-al.tldr: HyperDM estimates both data-reducible and inherent uncertainty with one model while achieving prediction accuracy comparable to multi-model ensembles.

paragraphs: A generated video can maintain consistent appearance and continuous content while still failing to express the activity requested by its text prompt. This paper argues that video dynamics deserve explicit evaluation alongside those existing criteria. Dynamics capture aspects of visual vividness and whether the changing content is faithful to the prompt.

The proposed protocol, DEVIL, measures dynamics at multiple temporal granularities. It also introduces a prompt benchmark with different grades of dynamics, creating a basis for assessing how broadly a model can vary activity and how well that activity matches the text. These measurements make motion-related behavior a direct target of evaluation.

The authors additionally study how existing evaluation metrics relate to dynamics and improve those metrics from this perspective. In experiments, DEVIL's metrics achieve up to approximately 90% consistency with human ratings. That upper reported agreement supports their potential usefulness, rather than establishing uniform agreement for every metric. The contribution is an evaluation framework that makes a previously underemphasized dimension of generated video more measurable.
neurips-2024-evaluation-of-text-to-video.tldr: DEVIL evaluates generated videos through their dynamics and alignment with prompts, with reported human-rating consistency reaching about 90%.

paragraphs: This paper studies how many samples are needed to find a policy whose long-run average reward is within epsilon of optimal. Two complexity measures matter: the diameter D and optimal bias span H, with H no larger than D. An earlier sample-efficient method required knowing H beforehand, raising the question of whether that knowledge could simply be estimated.

The authors prove that the samples needed to estimate H cannot be bounded by any function of the state count S, action count A, and H alone. They instead estimate the diameter and develop a policy-identification algorithm requiring no prior MDP knowledge. With a generative model, its sample complexity scales as SAD divided by epsilon squared for small epsilon, a near-optimal rate.

The online setting has a separate obstacle: a lower bound rules out sample complexity polynomial in H. The proposed online algorithm instead scales as SAD squared in D, namely SAD² divided by epsilon squared. The paper also introduces a data-dependent stopping approach as a promising direction for reducing that bound, without claiming that improvement is established.
neurips-2024-finding-good-policies-in-av.tldr: Diameter estimation enables near-optimal policy identification without prior MDP knowledge under generative access, with separate guarantees and lower bounds for online learning.

paragraphs: Learning actions from visual observations creates difficult exploration and exploitation problems because the state information is high-dimensional. Consistency models offer a time-efficient diffusion approach and had already been used in online reinforcement learning with state inputs. This paper investigates whether consistency policies can also work effectively when the agent learns from visual inputs.

The authors examine how changing data distributions and the actor-critic framework affect consistency-policy training. They find instability, particularly in visual reinforcement learning. To address it, they introduce sample-based entropy regularization for training stability and propose prioritized proximal experience regularization to improve sample efficiency. The combined method is called CP3ER.

CP3ER reports new state-of-the-art performance on 21 tasks across the DeepMind Control Suite and Meta-World. These results provide empirical support for extending consistency policies to the visual setting through changes to their training. The authors describe it as the first application of diffusion or consistency models to visual reinforcement learning to their knowledge, and present the findings as evidence of these models' potential in that setting.
neurips-2024-generalizing-consistency-po.tldr: CP3ER stabilizes consistency-policy training and improves sample efficiency, reporting leading results across 21 visual reinforcement learning tasks.

paragraphs: Evaluating a single answer does not fully capture how useful an assistant is during an information-seeking conversation. A model can be accurate yet fail to be the one people prefer interacting with. IQA-EVAL addresses this gap by evaluating interactive question answering while reducing reliance on costly, time-consuming human evaluation.

Its central component is an LLM-based Evaluation Agent, or LEA. The agent both simulates human behavior to create interactions with a question-answering model and evaluates the resulting conversations. The framework can assign personas to these agents to better represent groups of human evaluators, bringing differences among people into the automated evaluation process.

Using GPT-4 or Claude as its backbone, the framework shows high correlation with human evaluations on the interactive task. Adding personas further improves those correlations significantly. The authors then evaluate five recent language models on more than 1,000 complex and ambiguous questions, an evaluation estimated to cost $5,000 with humans. These findings support automated conversational evaluation that tracks human judgments in the studied setting.
neurips-2024-iqa-eval-automatic-evaluati.tldr: IQA-EVAL uses persona-equipped language-model agents to simulate and assess question-answering conversations with strong human-evaluation correlation.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph completion predicts missing relationships, and this paper treats it as completing a three-way binary tensor. Tensor decomposition models are effective for this task, but their expressive power also creates a tendency to overfit. The authors begin by deriving a general form that brings existing models into a shared framework.

They then propose a different target for regularization. Existing approaches constrain the sizes of embeddings; the new method constrains intermediate variables arising in different ways of computing the predicted tensor. This shifts the regularization toward quantities involved in constructing the prediction. The method applies to most tensor decomposition models while keeping computation tractable.

The theoretical analysis shows that this regularization promotes a low trace norm for the predicted tensor, providing a mathematical explanation for its role in reducing overfitting. Experiments support both the method's effectiveness and the theoretical account. The contribution combines a common description of existing models with a broadly applicable way to control their predictions through internal computation.
neurips-2024-knowledge-graph-completion-.tldr: Regularizing intermediate computations helps tensor-based knowledge graph models reduce overfitting, with theoretical and experimental support.

paragraphs: People often have useful knowledge about a prediction problem but lack the expertise to encode it in a probabilistic model. This paper explores a regression interface where numerical observations and natural-language descriptions jointly guide predictions. The goal is to predict distributions at arbitrary locations, allowing users to express prior knowledge in ordinary language.

The authors investigate how to prompt language models for explicit, coherent joint numerical predictive distributions, which they call LLM Processes. Considering quantities jointly matters because the intended output describes their collective uncertainty. They examine these distributions in forecasting, multidimensional regression, black-box optimization, and image modeling, while studying the prompting details needed to elicit coherence.

The reported results demonstrate effectiveness at regression and show that text can improve numerical predictive performance. Qualitative descriptions also produce corresponding quantitative structure in the predictions. This supports using language models as an interface for user expertise and as a possible source of relevant knowledge already encoded in the model, opening a way to explore that knowledge through numerical predictions.
neurips-2024-llm-processes-numerical-pre.tldr: LLM Processes turn numerical observations and natural-language prior knowledge into coherent joint predictive distributions.

paragraphs: LuSh-NeRF reconstructs a clean, sharp scene representation from handheld photographs taken in low light. Such images can combine poor visibility, noise, and camera-shake blur. The paper argues that these effects are strongly coupled, so directly combining existing low-light and motion-handling methods, or adding image enhancement, does not adequately solve the problem.

The approach follows an observation about image formation: low-light noise remains sharp even when camera motion blurs the scene. This suggests an order among the degradation processes that can help separate them. LuSh-NeRF models noise and blur sequentially during training, using consistency across views for noise and frequency information for blur.

A Scene-Noise Decomposition module separates noise from the scene representation. A Camera Trajectory Prediction module estimates camera movement using low-frequency scene information. The authors also construct a dataset containing synthetic and real images for training and evaluation. Experiments report better performance than existing approaches, supporting the value of respecting the order and coupling of image degradation when reconstructing low-light scenes.
neurips-2024-lush-nerf-lighting-up-and-s.tldr: LuSh-NeRF separates noise and camera-motion blur during training to reconstruct clean, sharp scenes from handheld low-light photographs.

paragraphs: Tandem mass spectrometry provides high-throughput measurements used to investigate molecular structures, but interpreting a spectrum remains difficult even for experts. Most acquired spectra therefore remain uninterpreted. MassSpecGym addresses a development bottleneck for machine learning in this area: the lack of shared datasets and evaluation protocols for comparing methods.

The benchmark brings together what the authors describe as the largest publicly available collection of high-quality tandem mass spectra. It organizes evaluation around three tasks: generating molecular structures from scratch, retrieving molecules, and simulating spectra. These tasks provide distinct ways to study the relationship between molecular structures and their measured spectral information.

MassSpecGym also supplies new evaluation metrics and a data split designed to demand generalization. Together, the dataset, tasks, and evaluation rules establish a common framework for method development. Its contribution is research infrastructure for molecular discovery and identification, making these problems more accessible to the broader machine learning community and giving researchers a standardized basis for evaluating progress.
neurips-2024-massspecgym-a-benchmark-for.tldr: MassSpecGym standardizes molecular structure generation, molecule retrieval, and spectrum simulation with shared mass-spectrometry data and evaluation protocols.

paragraphs: Some learning problems constrain their solutions to a curved mathematical space called a manifold. Principal component analysis and low-rank matrix completion are examples motivating this paper. The authors study the federated version of such optimization, where clients have heterogeneous data and the objective can be nonconvex.

The proposed algorithm operates on a compact smooth submanifold. It combines stochastic Riemannian gradients, which account for the manifold's geometry, with a projection operator. Local updates reduce communication, while the algorithm also avoids client drift. These components address both the geometric constraints of the problem and the costs of learning across clients with different data.

The analysis jointly uses the manifold structure and properties of the loss functions. It establishes sublinear convergence to a neighborhood of a first-order optimal solution, rather than guaranteeing an exact or globally optimal solution. Numerical experiments report substantially lower computation and communication overhead than existing methods. The result offers an efficiency-oriented federated algorithm with a convergence guarantee tailored to the stated geometric setting.
neurips-2024-nonconvex-federated-learnin.tldr: A geometry-aware federated algorithm reduces computational and communication overhead while converging toward a neighborhood of a first-order solution.

paragraphs: Plant-and-Steal studies fair allocation of indivisible goods when agents have additive valuations and incentives to report strategically. Its fairness target is the maximin share, or MMS. Truthfulness makes approximation harder: good allocation algorithms alone do not resolve the incentive problem. The paper asks how predictions about preferences can improve truthful mechanisms.

For two agents, the mechanism uses predicted item rankings. Accurate predictions yield a 2-approximation to MMS, while incorrect predictions still retain a ceiling-of-m/2 approximation for m items. Its performance also degrades gradually with the number of prediction mistakes, interpolating up to constant factors between the accurate and maximally mistaken cases.

The authors additionally prove a limit on achievable consistency for mechanisms with finite robustness. For any number of agents at least two, they give a 2-approximation mechanism under accurate predictions, with weaker fallback guarantees. Experiments illustrate when the components supporting accurate-prediction performance and robustness become relevant. The work therefore treats prediction quality as a variable that shapes fairness guarantees while retaining the incentive requirements.
neurips-2024-plant-and-steal-truthful-fa.tldr: Predicted preference rankings improve truthful fair allocation, with guarantees that degrade gracefully as prediction errors increase.

paragraphs: Graph neural network defenses can appear secure until strong adaptive attacks expose weaknesses. This paper examines representative robust graph neural networks through a shared statistical lens: robust estimation. That perspective is used to explain both the robustness these methods achieve and the limitations that remain in their estimation behavior.

The analysis focuses on estimation bias and motivates a graph signal estimator designed to be both robust and unbiased. The authors develop an efficient algorithm combining Quasi-Newton optimization with iterative reweighted least squares to solve the estimation problem. They then unfold its computational steps into aggregation layers for graph neural networks.

This construction connects the network's aggregation operation directly to the proposed estimation procedure and comes with theoretical guarantees. Comprehensive experiments report strong robustness across multiple scenarios, while an ablation study investigates the sources of the method's advantages. The contribution is a linked analysis-and-design approach: diagnose bias in existing robust aggregation, formulate an estimator that addresses it, and translate the solver into a usable neural architecture.
neurips-2024-robust-graph-neural-network.tldr: A robust, unbiased graph signal estimator becomes neural aggregation layers with theoretical guarantees and strong reported adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: When high-quality target data are expensive, additional training examples may come from different conditions or generative models. This paper calls those examples surrogate data and studies how to combine them with a smaller target dataset. The central method is weighted empirical risk minimization, which controls how much each data source influences training.

The authors analyze this method under several classical statistical models and test their findings on datasets from different domains. They find that surrogate data can substantially lower test error on the target distribution. Surprisingly, improvement can occur even with unrelated surrogate data, a phenomenon they connect to Stein's paradox. This is a possible benefit, not a claim that arbitrary added data always help.

Obtaining the benefit depends crucially on choosing optimal weights. The paper also finds that an approximate scaling law describes test error for models trained on mixtures of target and surrogate data. That relationship can guide both the weighting scheme and the amount of surrogate data to add, linking data acquisition decisions to expected predictive performance.
neurips-2024-scaling-laws-for-learning-w.tldr: An approximate scaling law helps choose how much surrogate data to add and how strongly to weight it for improved target-distribution predictions.

paragraphs: Agents trained together can develop communication protocols that solve a task well yet remain difficult to interpret. This paper asks what makes such communication meaningful beyond successful coordination. It introduces semantic consistency: the requirement that messages carry similar meanings across instances, framed independently of the particular task goal.

The authors formalize that property and compare two common training objectives, discrimination and reconstruction. Under mild assumptions, they prove that semantically inconsistent protocols can be optimal for discrimination but cannot be optimal for reconstruction. This shows that task success alone has different implications depending on the objective used to train communication.

Reconstruction also encourages a stronger property called spatial meaningfulness, which takes distances between messages into account. Experiments with emergent communication games support the theoretical results. The findings give a reason to favor distance-based communication goals when consistent meaning matters, while keeping the theoretical comparison tied to its assumptions. They also help explain why earlier experiments could observe counterintuitive protocols despite nearly perfect task performance.
neurips-2024-semantics-and-spatiality-of.tldr: Under mild assumptions, reconstruction objectives rule out semantically inconsistent optimal communication protocols that discrimination objectives can permit.

paragraphs: Editing knowledge in a multimodal language model requires balancing several goals: making the intended change reliably, having it generalize, and preserving locality. Existing approaches either edit intrinsic knowledge or resort to external knowledge, each with strengths and weaknesses. UniKE proposes a unified framework for working with both forms of knowledge.

The method represents intrinsic and external knowledge as vectorized key-value memories. This places their editing processes at the same semantic level and describes them through an analogy to assimilation and accommodation in human cognition. The shared representation provides a basis for coordinating approaches that otherwise operate through different knowledge sources.

Within that framework, UniKE separates knowledge representations into semantic and truthfulness spaces to promote collaboration. Extensive experiments report that edited models maintain strong reliability, generality, and locality simultaneously. The findings support combining internal and external knowledge handling within one editing method, with the representation split providing an additional mechanism for their cooperation. The contribution concerns both a common conceptual treatment of editing and an implemented method evaluated against its desired properties.
neurips-2024-towards-unified-multimodal-.tldr: UniKE unifies internal and external knowledge editing through shared memory representations and separate semantic and truthfulness spaces.

paragraphs: Dense video streams create many visual tokens, increasing memory and computation demands in vision-language models. Reducing the number of tokens can help, but the paper argues that existing reduction approaches overlook context already modeled by the language model and may miss cues relevant to a user's query. VideoLLM-MoD targets the computation spent processing those tokens.

The method learns to let a high proportion of visual tokens bypass selected transformer layers and pass directly onward. For example, it can skip processing 80% of visual tokens at a particular layer. Keeping the tokens while varying their computational depth allows the model to exploit redundancy without reducing the visual token count.

The authors report approximately 42% training-time savings and 30% memory savings for the entire training process. Performance is preserved or improved relative to the vanilla model. Experiments also report state-of-the-art results on multiple narration, forecasting, and summarization benchmarks involving COIN, Ego4D, and Ego-Exo4D. These results support selective layer computation as an efficiency strategy for long-duration and streaming video.
neurips-2024-videollm-mod-efficient-vide.tldr: VideoLLM-MoD lets visual tokens skip selected layers, cutting training time and memory while preserving or improving evaluated performance.

paragraphs: Retrieval can give a language model useful evidence, but retrieved passages may contradict each other even when they come from the same trusted source. WikiContradict examines whether models communicate those disagreements accurately. Its target is an answer that presents the conflicting perspectives, rather than simply selecting one of them.

The benchmark contains 253 human-annotated instances based on contradictory Wikipedia passages. The authors evaluate open and closed models under different question-answering conditions, including one retrieved passage and two conflicting passages. Human evaluation of a subset covers five models and more than 3,500 judgments, providing evidence about how their answers handle these conflicts.

All models in that human evaluation struggled to reflect contradictory context accurately, particularly when recognizing the conflict required reasoning. To reduce evaluation cost, the authors also develop an automated evaluator using a strong open-source language model, reporting an F-score of 0.8. They use it to assess more than 1,500 answers from seven models across the full benchmark. The work makes conflict acknowledgment an explicit, measurable component of retrieval-augmented answering.
neurips-2024-wikicontradict-a-benchmark-.tldr: WikiContradict tests whether language models explain conflicting retrieved evidence and finds persistent difficulties, especially with implicit contradictions.

paragraphs: xRAG compresses retrieved context by using a document's dense retrieval embedding in place of its text. These embeddings ordinarily help find relevant documents; the paper instead treats them as a separate information modality that can be connected to a language model. This enables an extremely compact, one-token representation of retrieved context.

A trainable modality bridge maps the document embeddings into the language model's representation space. Both the retriever and the language model remain frozen. This design lets xRAG reuse document embeddings computed offline while keeping retrieval augmentation modular, with training concentrated in the component that connects the two existing systems.

Experiments report an average improvement above 10% across six knowledge-intensive tasks and compatibility with backbones ranging from a dense 7B model to an 8x7B mixture-of-experts model. The method outperforms previous context-compression approaches and matches uncompressed performance on several datasets, while reducing overall floating-point operations by a factor of 3.53. The results support feeding retrieval representations directly into generation as an efficient alternative to processing the retrieved text.
neurips-2024-xrag-extreme-context-compre.tldr: xRAG connects existing document embeddings to a frozen language model, achieving one-token context compression with strong reported accuracy and computational savings.
